subtype: Approach: accepting the first offer from fear of losing it [Pitfall]
passage:
Yash: You started in March too, right? Same level as me?
Hansa: Yes. Level two.
Yash: What did they offer you? I only ask because I found out they told me a lot more than I expected.
Hansa: I didn't ask. They phoned on Friday and I said yes before they'd finished the sentence. I thought if I hesitated it would disappear.
Yash: Nothing at all? Not one question?
Hansa: Not one. I could have asked about a joining bonus, or a review. I keep thinking about that.
Yash: Mine is quite a bit more than you told me yours is.
Hansa: I know. I saw the pay slip mix-up. It stung.
Yash: It's done. But next time, ask one thing. Only one.
Hansa: One. Okay.

qa.q: When did the company phone Hansa with the offer?
qa.a: The company phoned Hansa on Friday.

qa.q: What is Hansa feeling now about accepting so fast?
qa.a: Hansa feels regret and a sting, thinking that even one question should have been asked.

qa.q: What could Hansa do next time, and why?
qa.a: Hansa could ask one clear question, such as about a joining bonus or a review, because asking rarely makes an offer vanish and can improve it.

qa.q: How might Yash feel about telling Hansa?
qa.a: Yash probably feels awkward and sympathetic, wanting to help Hansa learn from it rather than feel worse.

grounding: Illustrates accepting the first offer at once for fear of losing it, then learning colleagues at the same level were paid more and regretting not asking.
